To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Escherichia. coli Sequence type 131 (ST131), a globally successful multidrug-resistant pathogen, is a major cause of bloodstream and urinary tract infection in the United States.

Escherichia Coli Sequence Type 131 is an emerging cause of bloodstream infections in the United States, that it has a high rate of resistance to antibiotics, that it is associated with a higher mortality rate compared to other bloodstream infections and that it is associated more with the urinary tract rather than with the gastrointestinal tract, which is the most common site of infection.

the whole genome sequence-based phylogeny of E. coli ST131 from a cohort of six households in a low-income urban neighborhood in the U.S. Midwest supported the fecal–urethral hypothesis of ST131 transmission and confirmed within-households strain sharing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the whole genome of the bacterium Escherichia Coli (E. coli).

the development of a novel method for the analysis of the whole genome sequences of Escherichiacoli, which allows the identification of the most important genetic features of these bacteria and their role in the evolution of the strains.
the development of an integrated system for the detection, identification and quantification of E. coli O157 in meat and other foodstuffs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ST131 H30R1 and the H30Rx clades are the most common ST131 sublineages in North America.
the ST131 lineage, which is a major cause of multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections, is not a single clonal complex but a diverse lineage of clones that are closely related to each other.

E. coli ST131 is a highly successful, globally dispersed, and genetically diverse pathogen that is capable of colonizing the gastrointestinal tract of humans and animals, causing urinary tract infection, and disseminating to other sites, such as the bloodstream.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fecal-urinary hypothesis is a reasonable explanation for the spread of E. coli ST131 in households.
we found that the fecal-urinary hypothesis holds for ST131 and that there is a lot of diversity within this clonal complex.
the ST131 lineage of E. coli has evolved to be an important cause of urinary tract and bloodstream infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now use whole-genome sequencing to study the transmission of ST131 within households, which is not possible with traditional molecular typing methods.
we have shown that the ST131 lineage is not only a major cause of urinary tract infections, but is also associated with asymptomatic bacteriuria in the community.
the fecal-oral route of transmission is the most important mode of transmission for E. coli in the household setting.
